subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Yellow Dwarfs: Stars Like Our Sun
description: One-minute skill: Yellow Dwarfs: Stars Like Our Sun.

hook.text: Our Sun is a G-type yellow dwarf—medium-sized, medium-temperature, and perfectly ordinary.

buildup.text: Yellow dwarfs live about 10 billion years. Hot enough for habitable planets, stable enough for life to evolve.

discovery.text: They fuse hydrogen at their cores at about 15 million °C, producing steady light and heat for billions of years.

twist.text: Yellow dwarfs are relatively rare—only about 7% of all stars. Red dwarfs vastly outnumber them.

climax.text: Alpha Centauri A is another yellow dwarf, just 4.37 light-years away. A possible twin of our own Sun.

punchline.text: Ordinary, stable, rare. The perfect star for life around it.

quiz.question: What percentage of stars are yellow dwarfs like our Sun?

details.summary: Yellow dwarfs (G-type main-sequence stars) like our Sun have surface temperatures around 5,500°C and lifetimes of about 10 billion years. They're massive enough to produce substantial energy but stable enough for billions of years of consistent output — ideal for nurturing life on orbiting planets.
details.whyItMatters: Our Sun is a yellow dwarf, making this stellar type directly relevant to understanding Earth's habitability. Its stable energy output for billions of years gave life time to evolve from microbes to complex civilization.
takeaways: Yellow dwarfs have surface temperatures around 5,500°C
They live about 10 billion years with stable energy output
Their stability makes them ideal for hosting habitable planets

faq.question: Is our Sun actually yellow?
faq.answer: The Sun's peak emission is actually green-white. It appears yellow from Earth's surface because the atmosphere scatters blue light. From space, the Sun looks white. The name 'yellow dwarf' comes from its classification color on the HR diagram, not its actual perceived color.

faq.question: How common are Sun-like stars?
faq.answer: About 7-8% of stars in our galaxy are G-type like the Sun. They're less common than red dwarfs (75% of stars) but more common than larger, brighter types. Billions of Sun-like stars exist in the Milky Way, many potentially hosting habitable planets.
